card: Paper card. Question: How can strong local compositional disorder in high entropy oxides be exploited to generate tunable magnetic behaviors, ranging from macroscopically ordered states to frustration-driven dynamic spin interactions, and can a simplified model predict the emergence of these states?. System: La(Cr0.2Mn0.2Fe0.2Co0.2Ni0.2)O3 (L5BO) and Mn-varied variants La(Cr0.15Mn0.4Fe0.15Co0.15Ni0.15)O3 (40% Mn) and La(Cr0.1Mn0.6Fe0.1Co0.1Ni0.1)O3 (60% Mn). Processing: Pulsed laser epitaxy (PLD) on SrTiO3 (STO) and (La0.3Sr0.7)(Al0.65Ta0.35)O3 (LSAT) substrates; films were single-phase, epitaxial, with thicknesses of 56 nm (40% Mn), 58 nm (60% Mn), 62 nm (20% Mn), and ~90 nm for neutron diffraction.. Test conditions: Neutron diffraction on single-crystal films and bulk powder; SQUID magnetometry (field-cooled vs. zero-field-cooled) from low temperatures up to 300 K; Monte Carlo simulations using a classical Heisenberg model.. Findings: L5BO (20% Mn) exhibits robust long-range G-type antiferromagnetic (AFM) ordering with a Néel temperature (T_N) near 180 K in single-crystal films.; Increasing Mn concentration to 40% creates a degenerate tipping point where both AFM and ferromagnetic (FM) phases are percolated, resulting in a horizontal exchange bias shift.; Increasing Mn concentration to 60% shifts the dominant phase to ferromagnetism with a Curie temperature (T_C) of approximately 160 K and no observable exchange bias.; The 20% Mn system shows a vertical loop shift due to uncompensated FM moments within a percolated AFM matrix.; The 40% Mn composition displays an incipient quantum critical point where AFM and FM signals grow simultaneously upon cooling.; A classical Heisenberg model populated with composite parameter states accurately predicted the magnetic phase diagram and critical temperatures.; Exchange bias behaviors, traditionally found in bilayer heterojunctions, were generated in monolithic single-crystal films by manipulating local spin disorder.. Mechanism: The authors argue that the high entropy oxide hosts a random distribution of spin (S) and exchange (J) interactions where the dominant magnetic phase is determined by the percolation of specific microstates. Increasing Mn concentration shifts the balance from AFM-dominant (Fe-O-Fe bonds) to FM-dominant (Mn-O-X bonds). At 40% Mn, the system reaches a state where both AFM and FM clusters percolate coherently, creating intrinsic frustration and uncompensated spins at the interface of these coexisting phases, which drives the exchange bias effect without the need for physical heterostructuring.. Limitations: The text notes that computationally intensive first-principles approaches are impractical for high entropy oxides due to the vast number of possible microstates (over 200 nearest neighbor combinations), necessitating the use of a simplified classical Heisenberg model rather than precise quantitative calculations.. Future work: The authors propose that manipulating local spin disorder can be used to design novel Griffiths phases or quantum many-body systems with tunable critical behaviors, and that replacing geometric frustration with exchange frustration on a square lattice may lead to unexpected phase spaces.. Quote: "Single‐crystal La(Cr0.2Mn0.2Fe0.2Co0.2Ni0.2)O3 films are used as a model system hosting a magnetic sublattice with a high degree of microstate disorder in the form of site‐to‐site spin and exchange type inhomogeneity."
W4211194462.title: Designing Magnetism in High Entropy Oxides

card: Paper card. Question: Can configurational entropy be engineered to stabilize a single-phase solid solution in a five-component oxide system where the constituent binary oxides do not form solid solutions, and can this transition be reversed?. System: Equimolar mixture of MgO, CoO, NiO, CuO, and ZnO (labeled E1). Processing: Solid-state synthesis: powders milled for 2 h, pressed into pellets at 31,000 N, fired in air at temperatures ranging from 700 to 1,100 °C with 50 °C increments, and quenched; thin films prepared via pulsed laser deposition at 600 °C with 3 J cm⁻² energy density.. Test conditions: X-ray diffraction (XRD) monitoring phase evolution from 700 to 1,100 °C; differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and in situ XRD at 5 °C min⁻¹; EXAFS at Advanced Photon Source 12-BM-B; STEM-EDS analysis at 200 kV.. Findings: Full conversion to a single-phase rocksalt structure occurs between 850 and 900 °C, with no additional peaks observed above this range.; Removing any single component from the five-component mixture results in a multiphase material when equilibrated at 875 °C for 12 h.; Deviations from equimolarity by ±2, ±6, and ±10% increase the transition temperature to single phase, confirming the entropic driving force.; The phase transformation from multiphase to single phase is endothermic, with a measured enthalpy change of approximately 12 kJ mol⁻¹ (±2 kJ mol⁻¹).; EXAFS data shows cation-to-anion first-neighbour distances are identical within ±0.01 Å for Zn, Ni, Cu, and Co, consistent with random distribution.; STEM-EDS mapping reveals chemically and structurally homogeneous material with no evidence of phase separation or clustering at the atomic scale.; A small mass loss of approximately 1.5% occurs at the transition due to the reduction of 3+ to 2+ cations during the conversion of spinel intermediates to rocksalt.. Mechanism: The authors argue that the high configurational entropy of the five-component equimolar mixture overcomes the positive enthalpic penalties associated with structural transitions (specifically for CuO and ZnO) and mixing, stabilizing the single-phase solid solution at elevated temperatures. The entropy term (TΔS) in the Gibbs free energy becomes dominant, driving the reversible transition from a multiphase state to a random solid solution where cations occupy a single sublattice homogeneously.. Limitations: The authors note that quantitative calorimetry presents challenges, and the assumption of ideal mixing for enthalpy calculations is a simplification; literature reports indicate finite and mixed-sign enthalpies of mixing that are not fully captured by the reference transition enthalpy values.. Future work: The authors propose that entropic stabilization should be explored in other systems with intermediate anions, such as chalcogenides, nitrides, and halides, particularly where covalent character is modest, and call for rigorous theoretical exploration of the crystallographic model where intermediate anions render cation sites energetically equivalent.. Quote: "entropy predominates the thermodynamic landscape, and drives a reversible solid-state transformation between a multiphase and single-phase state."

card: Paper card. Question: Can tensile strain induce a high-temperature ferromagnetic insulator state in undoped, high-symmetry LaCoO3 thin films, and how do oxygen vacancies and Co2+ defects affect this state?. System: LaCoO3 thin films (nearly stoichiometric) grown on (001) SrTiO3 and (001) LSAT substrates; Co2+ defect concentration varied from 0% to ~25%. Processing: Pulsed-laser deposition at 750 °C with laser energy density ~1.5 J/cm2 and frequency 1 Hz; oxygen pressure varied between 1 Pa and 25 Pa; film thickness controlled via in situ RHEED oscillations (5 to 30 unit cells). Test conditions: Temperature range 4 K to 390 K for magnetization and resistivity; X-ray diffraction, STEM-HAADF, Co L-edge/K-edge XAS, XANES, and oxygen K-edge STEM-EELS; DFT calculations with GGA+U (U=5.27 eV, J=1.47 eV) at 3.5% tensile strain. Findings: Tensile-strained LaCoO3 films exhibit a ferromagnetic transition with a Curie temperature (TC) up to 90 K, significantly higher than the ≤16 K of known undoped high-symmetry ferromagnetic insulators.; The ferromagnetic state is strongest in nearly stoichiometric films grown at 25 Pa oxygen pressure, where TC is approximately 85 K.; Reducing oxygen pressure from 25 Pa to 10–15 Pa causes a dramatic decrease in TC and magnetization due to reduced tensile strain and increased nonstoichiometry.; Reducing film thickness below 10 unit cells increases Co2+ defect density, causing TC and magnetization to drop drastically.; Ferromagnetism disappears when the Co2+ defect concentration reaches approximately 10% (1Ov/32Co), with magnetization dropping from 2 μB/Co to 1.6 μB/Co.; At a Co2+ concentration of 12.5% (1Ov/16Co), magnetization decreases dramatically to 0.2 μB/Co due to long-range antiferromagnetic coupling.; At 25% Co2+ concentration, magnetization is close to zero, consistent with a step-function behavior with an inflection point near 10% Co2+.; First-principles calculations confirm that oxygen vacancies introduce extra electrons generating HS Co2+ states that support antiferromagnetic superexchange, suppressing ferromagnetism.. Mechanism: Tensile strain stabilizes a ferromagnetic state in LaCoO3 by promoting high-spin Co3+ ions and enabling ferromagnetic coupling between nearest high-spin and low-spin Co3+ ions. Oxygen vacancies introduce extra electrons that form high-spin Co2+ ions with half-occupied eg orbitals, which support antiferromagnetic superexchange interactions that suppress the ferromagnetic order. The ferromagnetism is robust only when Co2+ concentration is below ~10%; beyond this threshold, long-range antiferromagnetic coupling dominates.. Limitations: The detailed understanding of why the LaCoO3 Curie temperature is surprisingly high relative to other undoped high-symmetry ferromagnetic insulators is not yet clear. The nature of the ferromagnetic insulator state in LaCoO3 films remains partially unresolved regarding the specific roles of strain and oxygen vacancies in different contexts.. Future work: Further exploration is required to achieve a detailed understanding of the high Curie temperature behavior. The results provide a foundation for the growth and design of next-generation quantum-spintronic devices.. Quote: "Here we demonstrate a tensile-strained LaCoO3 film to be a strain-induced high-temperature ferromagnetic insulator."

card: Paper card. Question: How does entropy stabilization in transition-metal-based high entropy oxides (TM-HEO) influence reversible lithium storage capacity, cycling stability, and the underlying reaction mechanism compared to medium entropy oxides?. System: Transition-metal-based high entropy oxides (TM-HEO) with composition (Co0.2Cu0.2Mg0.2Ni0.2Zn0.2)O; compared to 4-cation medium entropy oxides (MEO) such as (Co0.25Cu0.25Zn0.25Ni0.25)O and (Co0.25Cu0.25Mg0.25Zn0.25)O. Processing: Nebulized Spray Pyrolysis (NSP) at 1150 °C; 4-cation systems required post-annealing at 1000 °C for 1 h under ambient atmosphere; electrodes cast with 63 wt% active material, 22 wt% Super C65, 15 wt% PVA binder. Test conditions: Galvanostatic cycling in Li-metal coin cells, voltage range 0.01–3 V vs. Li+/Li, specific currents from 50 to 3000 mA g−1, room temperature, 1 M LiPF6 in EC/DMC or EC/EMC electrolyte. Findings: The 5-cation TM-HEO cycled over 300 cycles at 200 mA g−1 with specific capacities stabilizing around 650 mAh g−1 after initial activation.; The 5-cation system achieved a specific capacity of 770 mAh g−1 after 100 cycles following a rate increase to 3 A g−1 for 5 cycles.; Medium entropy oxides (4-cation systems) showed rapid capacity degradation, with the Co-removed variant failing completely after ~10 cycles.; The Coulombic efficiency of the 5-cation TM-HEO stabilized between 99.4% and 99.95% in the range of cycles 60–400.; The 4-cation system without Zn (TM-MEO(-Zn)) exhibited a two-step oxidation process at 1.7 V and 2.2 V, unlike the single-step oxidation of the 5-cation system.; High-loading electrodes (2.3 mg cm−2) maintained Coulombic efficiencies >98.5% and an areal capacity of 1.3 mAh cm−2 after 30 cycles.; No metallic phases or Cu dendrites were detected via TEM/EDX after 100 cycles, despite the conversion reaction mechanism.. Mechanism: The authors propose that the rock-salt structure is preserved as a permanent host matrix during the entire conversion process. While some cations (e.g., Co, Cu) are reduced to metallic states during lithiation, they remain 'trapped' within the defect-rich rock-salt lattice stabilized by unreduced cations (e.g., Mg, Ni). This entropy stabilization lowers the Gibbs free energy, favoring the re-incorporation of reduced cations into the original lattice sites upon delithiation, preventing phase separation and structural collapse.. Limitations: The theoretical capacity cannot be predicted with high accuracy due to unknown additional processes like Zn-Li alloying or intermetallic formation; some 4-cation systems (TM-MEO(-Mg) and TM-MEO(-Ni)) could not be synthesized as single-phase compounds even at high temperatures.. Future work: Further investigations should be pursued to explore the full potential of high entropy oxide electrode materials, including the addition of other cations (Fe, Mn, Cr, V) to develop a modular method for tailoring electrodes to specific needs.. Quote: "The stabilization effect of entropy brings significant benefits for the storage capacity retention of high entropy oxides and greatly improves the cycling stability."

card: Paper card. Question: Can CoCrFeNiMo0.85 high-entropy alloy coatings, produced via mechanical alloying and electro spark deposition, provide effective corrosion resistance and adhesion for stainless steel substrates in aggressive geothermal environments?. System: CoCrFeNiMo0.85 high-entropy alloy deposited on 316 L stainless steel substrate. Processing: Solid-state processing: Mechanical alloying of high-purity Co, Cr, Fe, Ni, Mo powders for 30 h in a Pulverisette 6 Classic Line planetary ball mill (350 RPM, ball-to-powder ratio 10:1, N-Heptane process control agent) under Argon; cold pressing at 250 kN into 25 mm × 5 mm samples; sintering at 1100 °C for 1 h; machining into electrodes; electro spark deposition (ESD) under Argon atmosphere to deposit successive layers.. Test conditions: Pull-off testing per ASTM D4541–01; electrochemical corrosion testing in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution at 25 ± 0.5 °C for 6 h using potentiodynamic polarization.. Findings: Maximum adhesion resistance reached 0.67 MPa, limited by epoxy resin failure rather than coating-substrate interface failure.; Corrosion rate of the ESD coating calculated at 0.00016 mm/year in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution.; Polarization resistance of the coating was higher than 316 L stainless steel (22.50 kΩ × cm2).; XRD analysis revealed an increase in σ phase (rich in Co, Cr, Fe) and μ phase (rich in Mo) in the coating compared to the sintered electrode.; The coating microstructure showed a homogeneous and adhesive layer near the substrate, with slight porosity and splats in the upper part.; After corrosion testing, a passivation layer formed on the surface, covering most pores, containing an oxygen component likely from segregated chromium.; The open circuit potential (Eoc) was more electronegative than the bulk as-cast alloy, attributed to increased porosity delaying passivation.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the phase transformation (increase in σ and μ phases) to the rapid melting and cooling during the electro spark deposition process, driven by temperature differences and local solute solidification. The superior corrosion resistance is explained by the rapid formation of a passivation film, likely containing segregated chromium, which covers surface pores and reduces the corrosion current density significantly compared to bulk alloys or stainless steel.. Limitations: The coating is slightly porous in the upper part due to the BCC structure prone to pore formation in this high-entropy alloy and the ESD technique; the open circuit potential is more electronegative than the bulk alloy due to this porosity delaying passivation.. Future work: The authors state that novel promising coatings resistant to long-term high-temperature oxidation, corrosion action, and wear are currently being sought, implying further development is needed for these specific conditions.. card: Paper card. Question: How does the machinability of Al0.6CoCrFeNi high entropy alloy compare to 304 stainless steel in terms of cutting forces, tool wear, surface quality, and microstructural changes during milling?. System: Al0.6CoCrFeNi high entropy alloy (HEA) and X5CrNi18-10 (304) stainless steel. Processing: Face milling using a 12 mm diameter shank cutter with two indexable carbide inserts (grade HSC 05, PVTi coating) on a FIRST MCV 300 vertical milling center; dry cutting conditions; 25 tests using Taguchi method with cutting speed (vc), feed per tooth (fz), and axial depth of cut (ap) varied; radial depth of cut ae = 12 mm (100%); sample dimensions 145 × 15 × 6 mm³ for HEA. Test conditions: Dry cutting; spindle speeds up to 8000 rpm; feed rates up to 103 mm/min; axial depth of cut (ap) ranging from 0.1 mm to 0.42 mm; feed per tooth (fz) ranging from 0.05 mm/tooth to 0.15 mm/tooth; cutting speed (vc) varied across 5 levels; temperature measured via thermo vision camera (0–500 °C range); cutting forces measured with Kistler 9257B dynamometer. Findings: The machinability of the HEA was found to be about 59% better than that of 304 stainless steel based on the resultant cutting force.; Cutting temperatures ranged from 120 °C to 281 °C, with the maximum temperature (213.2 °C) recorded after about 6 s of processing.; The axial depth of cut (ap) was identified as the main influencing parameter on cutting temperature, with maximum temperatures (240–281 °C) occurring at ap = 0.42 mm.; Maximum flank wear width (VBB max) was 86 µm for the first cutting edge (CE1) and 67 µm for the second cutting edge (CE2).; Maximum crater dimensions on the rack face for CE2 were KBmax = 490 µm and KMmax = 225 µm.; Surface roughness values ranged from 0.39 µm to 2.058 µm, with the best values obtained at minimum feed (fz = 0.05 mm/tooth).; Microhardness of the machined HEA surfaces ranged from 365 HV0.2 to 444 HV0.2, attributed to material inhomogeneity and self-hardening.; XRD analysis showed that patterns for as-cast and machined surfaces were very similar, with no new phases formed during machining.. Mechanism: The superior machinability of the HEA compared to stainless steel is attributed to its specific cutting force behavior, where the resultant force is lower despite higher hardness. The irregular chip fragmentation and surface defects are caused by the inhomogeneity of the cast material and the presence of hard intermetallic phases (e.g., Fe2Al5, FeAl3) which act as micro-edges causing tool wear. Self-hardening effects and oxidation during cutting contribute to the increased microhardness and chip fragmentation, while the similar XRD patterns indicate the material withstands heating cycles without phase transformation.. Limitations: The study was limited to dry cutting conditions and did not evaluate the effects of cooling and lubrication. The research is described as preliminary, and the number of reference XRD patterns available in the database is limited. The study did not cover extended ranges of cutting parameters for finish and rough cuts, nor did it generate predictive mathematical models for material removal rate or tool life.. Future work: More detailed research should be achieved to have a more precise image of the machinability of the HEA by considering the cutting speed, material removal rate and cutting tool life. Furthermore, extended ranges of the cutting parameters should be considered for both finish cut and rough cut and to generate predictive mathematical models to improve processing and optimize cutting parameters.. Quote: "In terms of cutting forces, the behavior of the HEA was found to be about 59% better than that of stainless steel."

card: Paper card. Question: What are the thermal stability, phase transition temperatures, and microstructural evolution of the metastable intermetallic phases in the CoCrFeMo0.85Ni high-entropy alloy?. System: CoCrFeMo0.85Ni high-entropy alloy (gas atomized powder, nominal equimolar CoCrFeNi with 0.85 Mo). Processing: Gas atomization of high-purity Co, Cr, Fe, Mo, and Ni powders (approx. 24 µm); thermal analysis via DTA and DSC with 5 K/min heating/cooling cycles up to 1400 °C under Ar atmosphere; interrupted DTA at 900 °C; microstructural characterization via FEGSEM, EDX, and EBSD. Test conditions: Heating and cooling cycles at 5 K/min up to 1400 °C; interrupted heating at 900 °C; analysis of as-received powder, interrupted sample, and fully solidified sample. Findings: Solidus and liquidus temperatures determined as 1323 °C and 1331 °C, respectively.; Phase transitions observed at 800 °C (exothermal formation of intermetallics) and 1212 °C (endothermic dissolution).; As-received powder exhibits fine alternating layers suggesting spinodal-like morphology with minor elemental segregation.; After full thermal cycles, a dendritic microstructure forms with a single-phase FCC matrix.; The FCC matrix is depleted in Mo (<1/3 of dendrite content) and enriched in Ni compared to the dendrite core.; Dendrite cores contain a tetragonal (Co, Cr, Fe)-rich phase (presumed σ) surrounded by a Mo-rich rhombohedral phase (presumed µ).; The precipitation window for the cooling curve is identified between 780 °C and 1200 °C.; CALPHAD predictions show a single FCC phase above 1280 °C, which disagrees with DTA-derived liquidus at 1331 °C.. Mechanism: The formation of the FCC matrix is driven by high mixing entropy reducing Gibbs free energy. During solidification, Mo partitions to the liquid phase due to its high melting point and sluggish diffusion, segregating to interdendritic regions. The metastable phases (σ and µ) form via spinodal decomposition and compositional modulation driven by segregation, where Mo enrichment acts as a precursor state. The coexistence of σ and µ phases is attributed to cooperative diffusion and the order of elemental partitioning, with the µ phase growing at the periphery of the σ phase.. Limitations: The CALPHAD method may require further assessment for the transition temperatures of intermetallic formation in this HEA. The stabilization of the σ phase is a gradual process that is too slow to be fully observed in the DTA experiments due to kinetic effects. The study notes that the interaction of metastable phases in powder form can be eliminated by high-temperature treatment, limiting the observation of certain short-term phenomena.. Future work: Further detailed thermal analysis should be performed to derive remaining thermodynamic properties such as partial pressure and activity. Additional investigation of intermetallic phases is needed to facilitate understanding of atomic arrangement and orientation for optimal HEA design.. Quote: "Solidus and liquidus temperatures of CoCrFeMo0.85Ni were determined by differential thermal analysis as 1323 °C and 1331 °C, respectively."

card: Paper card. Question: How do laser metal deposited CoCrFeNiMo0.85 and Al0.5CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy coatings perform regarding erosion and corrosion resistance in three distinct geothermal environments, and how do manufacturing defects influence their degradation?. System: CoCrFeNiMo0.85 (Mo-HEA) and Al0.5CoCrFeNi (Al-HEA) coatings deposited on carbon steel (S235JR) and stainless steel (AISI 316L, 304L) substrates. Processing: Laser metal deposition (LMD) using a Trumpf Trudisk 8002 5.3 kW disc laser system, Reis RV60-40 robot, and Oerlikon-Metco 10-C powder feeder under argon atmosphere; coating thickness 800–1000 µm; no post-deposition grinding or polishing. Test conditions: Three environments at Hellisheidi geothermal site: (1) Wellhead test at 194 °C and 14 bar (deaerated); (2) Aerated test at 90 °C and 1 bar (fluid mixed with atmospheric gas); (3) Erosion test at 198 °C and 15 bar (high-velocity fluid impact at 90° angle). Findings: Mo-HEA coatings on carbon steel exhibited manufacturing cracks up to 50–60 µm deep, while Mo-HEA on stainless steel showed no cracks.; Al-HEA coatings were prone to general and localized corrosion damage in all tests, forming oxide-rich films 20–40 µm thick in the wellhead test.; In the erosion test, Al-HEA coatings developed erosion pits deeper than 100 µm after a 90-day exposure period.; Erosion pits in Mo-HEA coatings were observed only at the location of pre-existing vertical cracks, where fluid turbulence increased damage.; Mo-HEA coatings on stainless steel substrates showed no adhesion damage or cracking in any of the three test environments.; Galvanic corrosion products (iron-based) formed at the interface of Mo-HEA coatings and carbon steel substrates after exposure and ambient drying.; The oxide layer on Mo-HEA in the aerated test was discontinuous, likely due to Cr concentration gradients and sluggish diffusion rates.. Mechanism: Manufacturing cracks in Mo-HEA on carbon steel induce fluid turbulence that accelerates erosion; Al-HEA suffers from internal stresses and rapid oxidation kinetics of Al leading to non-passive, brittle oxide films; galvanic effects between noble Mo-HEA and carbon steel exacerbate corrosion at interfaces upon exposure to ambient air.. Limitations: The study notes that surface roughness measurements were inconclusive due to scaling dominance, and the statistical null hypothesis method for erosion assessment failed due to high variability in coating thickness.. Future work: The formulation and production of the CoCrFeNiMo0.85 coating need to be optimized to prevent cracking on carbon steel substrates; longer exposure periods are needed to verify if the discontinuous oxide layer on Mo-HEA becomes continuous.. Quote: "Wide manufacturing cracks are concluded to enhance the fluid-induced erosion effect for the CoCrFeNiMo0.85 coating in the vicinity of the cracks."

Question: How does the microstructure and phase stability of an equiatomic CrNiCoFeMn high-entropy alloy evolve during and after selective laser melting (SLM) and subsequent high-temperature annealing, and what is the impact on mechanical properties?. System: Equiatomic CrNiCoFeMn (Cantor alloy) produced from mechanically alloyed powders (purity >97 at.%). Processing: Selective Laser Melting (SLM) using SISMA MYSINT100 RM with Nitrogen atmosphere (O2 <0.5%), layer thickness H=0.05 mm, energy density F=200 J/mm3, recoating rate 70/150 mm/s, spot diameter 50 μm; followed by cold rolling (90% thickness reduction) and annealing at 723–1423 K for 25 h or 1170 K for 100 h. Test conditions: Microstructural analysis via XRD, SEM-FEG-EDS, and EBSD; mechanical testing via Vickers microhardness; annealing temperatures: 723, 823, 923, 1023, 1123, 1223, 1323, 1423 K. Findings: The as-built SLM alloy contains fine Cr-rich nitride and σ phase precipitates despite XRD showing a single FCC structure.; Precipitates increase in number and size after annealing between 900 K and 1300 K, with σ phase nucleating at grain boundaries and triple points.; At 1423 K, the σ phase and most nitrides dissolve, resulting in a single FCC structure with near-equieatomic composition.; Cold rolling followed by annealing accelerates recrystallization and σ phase precipitation compared to as-built samples.; Microhardness increases significantly after cold rolling and at low annealing temperatures (723–823 K) due to fine precipitates.; Hardness decreases progressively above 1023 K as σ phase grows and grains coarsen, following the Hall–Petch relationship.; The σ phase is tetragonal, Cr-rich (~50 at.%), and forms preferentially at grain boundaries and triple points during recrystallization.. Mechanism: Nitrogen interstitial diffusion during SLM leads to supersaturation and nitride nucleation; subsequent thermal cycles and rapid cooling promote heterogeneous nucleation of σ phase around nitrides. Recrystallization and increased diffusion rates at higher temperatures cause σ phase growth at boundaries, while very high temperatures (≥1423 K) enable dissolution back to a single FCC phase.. Limitations: The text states that distinguishing between Cr2N and CrN via EDS is difficult due to small precipitate size, and that the exact activation energy for precipitation requires further nucleation and coarsening studies.. Future work: Further experimental work focusing on nucleation and coarsening is required to fully understand the precipitation process; thermodynamic databases and models need to be extended to better understand this complex alloy behavior.. Quote: "The as-produced alloy shows fine nitride and σ phase precipitates, which are Cr-rich and stable up to about 900 K."

W1947673625.title: Quantification of sigma-phase evolution in thermally aged 2205 duplex stainless steel

card: Paper card. Question: How does the addition of 5 at. % Zr to a CoCrFeMnNi Cantor High Entropy Alloy affect its melting temperature, microstructure evolution during recrystallization, and mechanical properties when processed via vacuum induction melting of pre-alloyed powders?. System: Co20Cr20Fe20Mn20Ni20 (base) and Co19Cr19Fe19Mn19Ni19Zr5 (Zr-modified). Processing: Mechanical alloying of elemental powders for 45 h at 400 rpm; vacuum induction melting at >1720 K for 30 min; cold rolling to 90% thickness reduction; annealing at 1143 K (Zr-modified) or 1043 K (base) for 30 min. Test conditions: XRD (35°–100° 2Θ); SEM-EDS; TEM (200 kV); micro-hardness (300 mN and 50 mN loads); mechanical spectroscopy (400–900 Hz, room temp to 700 K at 1.5 K/min). Findings: The Zr-modified alloy exhibits a lower melting temperature due to eutectic formation, with liquid phase formation at about 1470 K compared to 2500 K for traditional arc melting.; The recrystallization temperature of the Zr-modified alloy (1143 K) is higher than that of the base alloy (1043 K).; After recrystallization, the Zr-modified alloy shows an average grain size of (6.0 ± 1.5) μm in dendritic regions and (1.5 ± 0.5) μm in inter-dendritic regions, compared to (15 ± 2) μm for the base alloy.; The Zr-modified alloy contains a coherent second phase (inter-dendritic) with an FCC structure, which is Ni-enriched and Zr-concentrated.; Micro-hardness of the Zr-rich inter-dendritic phase is higher than the dendritic region in as-cast and cold-rolled states, but both phases converge to similar values after recrystallization.; The dynamic Young's modulus at 300 K is (130 ± 10) GPa for the Zr-modified alloy versus (140 ± 10) GPa for the base alloy.; No cracks were observed in the Zr-modified alloy after cold rolling, indicating no significant embrittlement despite Zr addition.; Both alloys maintain an FCC crystallographic structure after annealing, with lattice parameters of (0.358 ± 0.002) nm for the Zr-modified alloy and (0.359 ± 0.002) nm for the base alloy.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the strengthening and grain refinement to the precipitation of a coherent second phase and the influence of Zr solute atoms on recovery and recrystallization processes. Solute atoms impede dislocation climb and cross-slip, leading to finer grains. The coherent nature of the second phase boundaries minimizes impediment to dislocation glide, preserving ductility while enhancing strength through precipitation and lattice distortion.. Limitations: The authors state that a more thorough investigation was not possible due to the limited amount of available material.. Future work: The authors propose that a more thorough investigation will be performed subsequently.. Quote: "A measure of 5 at. % Zr was added, resulting in a liquid phase formation at about 1470 K [,,], to be compared with the 2500 K of a traditional arc melting process."

W577352104.title: A selective laser melting and solution heat treatment refined Al–12Si alloy with a controllable ultrafine eutectic microstructure and 25% tensile ductility

card: Paper card. Question: How does Al alloying influence the tensile behavior, deformation mechanisms, and fracture modes of a Co-rich Co40Fe25Cr20Ni15 high-entropy alloy?. System: (Co40Fe25Cr20Ni15)100−xAlx with x = 0 and 5 at.%. Processing: Arc-melting raw elemental pellets, casting into a 50 mm × 20 mm × 4 mm mold, homogenization at 1423 K for 2 h, water quenching, cold-rolling with 70% thickness reduction, and recrystallization annealing at 973 K, 1023 K, and 1123 K for 2 h followed by water quenching.. Test conditions: Room-temperature tensile tests using a computer-controlled universal tensile testing machine at a strain rate of 10−4 s−1; Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations at 300 K.. Findings: The addition of 5 at.% Al increased the strength-ductility product (UTS × εf) from 19.2 GPa·% (0Al-1123 K) to 41.2 GPa·% (5Al-1123 K).; The 5Al-1123 K sample achieved a yield strength of 405 ± 4 MPa, tensile strength of 830 ± 3 MPa, and fracture elongation of ~50%.; The 0Al-973 K sample exhibited the highest yield strength of 612 ± 8 MPa but the lowest fracture elongation of ~15%.; The intrinsic stacking fault energy (SFE) increased from 70.6 mJ/m² in the 0Al alloy to 81.1 mJ/m² in the 5Al alloy.; The slip energy barrier (Δγ) decreased from 275 mJ/m² in the 0Al alloy to 228 mJ/m² in the 5Al alloy.; The twinning propensity ratio (Λratio) increased from 1.18 in the 0Al alloy to 1.29 in the 5Al alloy.; The fracture mode shifted from a mixture of quasi-cleavage and ductile-dimple (0Al) to exclusively ductile dimple (5Al).; The twin fraction in the 5Al-1123 K sample (~15.3%) was higher than in the 0Al-1123 K sample (~9.2%) at comparable local strains.. Mechanism: Al alloying increases the intrinsic SFE but reduces the slip energy barrier, which favors dislocation mobility and increases twinning propensity. This combination promotes prolonged strain hardening and delays necking, allowing for higher plastic strain accumulation and a transition to ductile dimple fracture, whereas the 0Al alloy suffers from high resistance to dislocation nucleation and limited slip mobility leading to early fracture.. Limitations: The authors note that the calculated SFE values (70.6 and 81.1 mJ/m²) are relatively high compared to the proposed experimental range for mechanical twinning (15 ≤ SFE ≤ 45 mJ/m²), attributing this discrepancy to factors like thermodynamic, magnetic, ordering, temperature, and pressure effects that are difficult to replicate in theoretical calculations.. Quote: "The addition of Al resulted in a massive improvement in the strength-ductility product, even at similar grain sizes, and also altered the fracture mode from quasi-cleavage to ductile dimple fracture."

card: Paper card. Question: How can a precipitation-strengthening strategy be used to design a high-entropy/medium-entropy alloy that sustains ultrahigh strength and excellent ductility simultaneously across a wide temperature range from cryogenic to elevated temperatures?. System: Al5(CoNiV)95 (at %) alloy, a CoNiV-based face-centered cubic (fcc)/B2 duplex medium-entropy alloy (MEA) with 5 at% Al added to an equiatomic fcc-structured CoNiV matrix; also Al7(CoNiV)93 for comparison. Processing: Arc-melting high-purity (>99.9 at%) Al, Co, Ni, and V metals followed by suction-casting into a Cu mold; homogenization at 1373 K for 8 hours with water quenching; cold rolling with 65% thickness reduction; annealing at 1173 K for 1 hour with water quenching. Test conditions: Uniaxial tensile tests at 77 K, 298 K, 723 K, and 1073 K using a universal testing machine at a fixed strain rate of 10⁻³ s⁻¹; microstructural analysis via XRD, EBSD, TEM, and synchrotron high-energy XRD on tensile-fractured samples. Findings: At room temperature (298 K), the alloy exhibited a yield strength of 1.1 GPa, ultimate tensile strength of 1.5 GPa, and tensile elongation of ~34%.; At cryogenic temperature (77 K), yield strength increased to 1.4 GPa, ultimate tensile strength to 1.9 GPa, with fracture elongation of ~38%.; At intermediate temperature (723 K), the alloy maintained a yield strength of 1.1 GPa with serrated stress-strain response and high strain hardening rates.; At high temperature (1073 K), the alloy showed enhanced ductility of ~74% and ultimate tensile strength of 0.28 GPa, attributed to dynamic recrystallization.; The alloy achieved the highest specific yield strength among reported ductile HEAs at ~150.2 MPa·cm³/g.; The volume fraction of the B2 phase in Al5(CoNiV)95 was estimated at ~6%, with B2 grain sizes ranging from several hundred nanometers to ~1 μm.; In the Al7(CoNiV)93 variant, increasing Al content raised the B2 phase volume fraction to ~21% and resulted in ~280% superplastic elongation at 1073 K.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the strength-ductility synergy to multiple deformation mechanisms: precipitation strengthening from Al-rich B2 nanoparticles; dynamic Hall-Petch effect where twin boundaries reduce dislocation mean free path; twinning-induced plasticity (TWIP) triggered by low stacking fault energy (SFE) in the fcc matrix; dynamic strain aging (DSA) at 723 K causing flow serrations; and dynamic recrystallization (DRX) enabling superplasticity at 1073 K. The B2 precipitates constrain the soft fcc matrix, generating back stresses, while twins mitigate interfacial stress concentrations to delay fracture.. Limitations: The authors note that the Al7(CoNiV)93 variant exhibited a ductile-brittle transition when lowering temperature from 298 to 77 K due to increased B2 precipitate density. Additionally, the superplastic elongation of the Al5(CoNiV)95 alloy (~74%) was insufficient compared to other microduplex alloys, attributed to deformation-enhanced grain growth which could be mitigated by using high strain rates.. Future work: The authors suggest that high strain rates could be used to overcome deformation-enhanced grain growth and improve superplastic elongation. They also propose that the design strategy can be adapted by adjusting Al content to optimize the balance between strength and ductility, and that combining chemical complexity with conventional strengthening principles can justify the industrial costs of M/HEAs.. Quote: "The ability of the alloy presented here to sustain this excellent strength-ductility synergy over a wide temperature range is aided by multiple deformation mechanisms i.e., twins, stacking faults, dynamic strain aging, and dynamic recrystallization."

card: Paper card. Question: How does the molten salt corrosion behavior of the dual-phase AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy compare to conventional duplex stainless steel 2205 in a NaCl-KCl-MgCl2 environment at high temperatures, and what are the underlying mechanisms?. System: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) and duplex stainless steel 2205 (DS2205). Processing: Vacuum-arc-melting of high purity constituent elements (99.95 wt.% purity) with multiple re-melting for homogeneity; samples polished to 1200-grit; molten salt prepared by annealing MgCl2, NaCl, and KCl (45.4, 33, 21.6 wt.% respectively) at 300 °C for 24 h in Ar atmosphere. Test conditions: Immersion in molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl2 salt at 450 °C and 650 °C for 24 hours; electrochemical measurements (OCP and potentiodynamic polarization) performed in open air. Findings: Corrosion rate of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 was ~1 mm/year at 450 °C compared to ~8 mm/year for DS2205.; Corrosion rate of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 was ~9 mm/year at 650 °C compared to ~20 mm/year for DS2205.; Mass loss for DS2205 at 650 °C was ~69 mg/cm² after 24 h, while AlCoCrFeNi2.1 was ~38 mg/cm².; Selective dissolution of the BCC phase (B2 in EHEA, α-Ferrite in DS2205) was observed in both alloys.; Cr depletion depth in AlCoCrFeNi2.1 at 650 °C was ~50 μm, significantly lower than ~300 μm for DS2205.; Volta potential difference between phases was ~50 mV for AlCoCrFeNi2.1 and ~35 mV for DS2205.; AlCoCrFeNi2.1 showed enrichment of Co and Ni in the near-surface region due to reduction of impurity ions.. Mechanism: The superior corrosion resistance of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 is attributed to the sacrificial role of Al which forms a redox couple (Al/AlCl3) that reduces the dissolution rate of Cr, Fe, and Ni, and the enrichment of noble elements (Co, Ni) in the protective surface layer. Micro-galvanic coupling between the phases drives selective dissolution of the less noble BCC phase, but the higher volume fraction of the nobler FCC phase and the thermodynamic stability of AlCl3 mitigate overall degradation compared to DS2205.. Limitations: A detailed evaluation of the effect of moisture content on corrosion behavior has not been performed in the current study.. Future work: The effect of moisture content on corrosion behavior is part of a future study.. Quote: "The EHEA showed a significantly lower corrosion rate of ~1 mm/year at 450 °C compared to ~8 mm/year for DS2205."

card: Paper card. Question: How to achieve a simultaneous balance of high fracture strength and high ductility in high-entropy alloys while overcoming inferior castability and compositional segregation?. System: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA). Processing: Vacuum induction melting of commercially pure elements (Al, Co, Ni: 99.9 wt.%; Cr, Fe: 99.5 ~ 99.6 wt.%) in a BN crucible; heating to 600°C for 1 hour; pouring at 1500°C into a MgO crucible (220 mm length, 62 mm upper ID, 50 mm bottom ID) under argon atmosphere (0.06 MPa); bulk ingot weight ~2.5 kg.. Test conditions: Room temperature tensile tests at strain rate 1 × 10−3 s−1; elevated temperature tests at 600°C and 700°C at strain rate 1 × 10−3 s−1; cold rolling with 8% thickness reduction followed by tensile testing at 2 × 10−3 s−1.. Findings: The as-cast alloy exhibited a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure with an inter-lamellar spacing of about 2 μm.; Room temperature tensile test showed a fracture stress of 944 MPa and an elongation of 25.6%.; The proof stress was 75 MPa, while the fracture stress reached close to 1.2 GPa (true stress condition).; At 600°C, the alloy maintained a fracture stress of 806 MPa and elongation of 33.7%.; At 700°C, the alloy maintained a fracture stress of 538 MPa and elongation of 22.9%.; Cold rolling with 8% reduction increased the true fracture stress to 1265 MPa while maintaining 9.9% elongation.; The density of the EHEA was measured to be 7.38 g/cm3.; The ratio of fracture strength to proof stress (σUTS/σ0.2) was close to 16.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the unprecedented strain hardening and balanced properties to the fine regular lamellar structure that easily stores dislocations and the alternating soft fcc phases and hard B2-structured NiAl-rich phases. When dislocations pass through soft fcc phases, the hard B2 phases, including nanoscale precipitates, pin the movement of dislocations resulting in significant work hardening.. Limitations: The text notes that the mechanism for the low elastic limit (proof stress) is still unclear at this stage.. Future work: Further exploration of new EHEAs will be based on physical metallurgy principles using atomic radius, mixing enthalpy, and valence electron concentration; thermodynamics calculations based on the CALPHAD method can provide guidance once reliable databases are established; the potential for producing ultrahigh strength components after large plastic deformation awaits further investigations.. Quote: "To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases."

card: Paper card. Question: What are the phase-specific mechanical behaviors, deformation mechanisms, and phase-boundary interactions in the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high entropy alloy under small-scale loading?. System: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high entropy alloy (lamellar arrangement of L12 and B2 solid-solution phases). Processing: Vacuum arc-melting of pure elements (>99.9% purity) with homogenization via multiple flips and re-melting cycles; samples polished to 0.02 µm roughness; micro-pillars prepared via FIB (30 kV Ga+ down to 5 kV) with final diameter 2.0 ± 0.3 µm and aspect ratio ~2; bulk specimens prepared via EDM (tensile) and machining (compression). Test conditions: Bulk tensile/compression at 10^-3 s^-1; nano-indentation at 10000 µN and 500 µN loads; strain rate sensitivity at 4×10^-2, 1.2×10^-1, and 4×10^-1 s^-1; micro-pillar compression at ~2.5×10^-4 s^-1; scratch tests at 500 mN load with ramping to 3000 µN. Findings: Ultimate tensile strength of 1165 ± 20 MPa with ~18% elongation; ultimate compressive strength of 1863 ± 12 MPa with ~34% fracture strain.; B2 phase showed higher hardness (7.5 ± 2.2 GPa at 500 µN) compared to L12 phase (6.0 ± 0.5 GPa).; B2 phase exhibited higher strain rate sensitivity (SRS) than L12, with bulk SRS close to B2 values.; Micro-pillar yield strength was ~610 MPa for B2 and ~460 MPa for L12; mixed pillars showed double yielding at ~350 MPa and ~620-640 MPa.; B2 phase deformed via plastic barreling with limited slip steps, while L12 phase showed high density of slip steps and homogeneous flow.; Coefficient of friction was ~0.89 for B2 and ~0.83 for L12; L12 showed more material pile-up during scratch tests.; Phase boundary remained preserved without separation or cracking even after high compressive strains in mixed micro-pillars.. Mechanism: The B2 phase controls deformation due to its higher strength and SRS, while the L12 phase accommodates plasticity through multiple slip systems. The semi-coherent phase boundary prevents crack propagation and separation, contributing to high strength and ductility. Cr-rich nano-precipitates (~20 nm) in the B2 phase act as barriers to dislocation movement, enhancing strength. The tension-compression asymmetry arises from lamellar orientation, elastic property differences, and volume fractions of the phases.. Limitations: The study notes that multiple yield points were not detected in bulk tests likely due to the small difference in modulus between phases and lower resolution of bulk experiments. The anisotropic behavior may depend on the location of samples due to varying cooling conditions in the ingot.. Future work: The authors state these results will pave the way for fundamental understanding of phase-specific contributions to bulk mechanical response and help in designing structural materials with high fracture toughness.. Quote: "Dual mode fracture was observed with ductile failure for L12 phase and brittle mode for B2 phase."

card: Paper card. Question: How does the elemental stability inherent in High Entropy Alloys (HEAs) due to high configurational entropy and/or sluggish diffusion affect elemental dissolution in molten fluoride salts, specifically regarding the corrosion performance and thermal stability of Cr18Mn27Fe27.5Ni27.5?. System: Cr18Mn27Fe27.5Ni27.5 High Entropy Alloy (FCC structure) and 316 H stainless steel (reference). Processing: Arc melting (Arcast Arc 200) followed by high-temperature homogenization at 1200 °C in a vacuum environment for 48 hours in quartz tubes with a titanium getter; samples exposed to molten FLiBe (2LiF-BeF2) at 700 °C for 1000 hours. Test conditions: Molten FLiBe salt at 700 °C for 1000 hours; salt purified by hydro-fluorination with H2/HF sparging; samples suspended in 316 L stainless steel capsules. Findings: The HEA experienced a mass loss of approximately 3.4 mg/cm2, significantly higher than the 0.26 mg/cm2 loss in 316 H stainless steel.; Mn concentration in the salt increased from 4 to 349 ppm after exposure to the HEA, indicating rapid Mn dissolution.; Cr concentration in the salt remained nearly unchanged (6 to 263 ppm in 316 H, negligible change in HEA), showing Cr retention in the HEA.; Mn depletion in the near-surface region of the HEA extended to a depth of approximately 40 µm.; A new BCC phase with nominal composition Cr67Fe13Mn18.5Ni1.5 precipitated, confirmed by bulk XRD and CALPHAD predictions.; The BCC phase fraction was predicted to be approximately 4% at 700 °C in the original alloy.; Needle-shaped Cr-rich particles were observed precipitating beneath the surface, with concentration varying with distance from the surface.. Mechanism: Mn acts as a sacrificial element due to its lower standard Gibbs free energy of formation for MnF2 compared to CrF2 and its higher diffusion coefficient; the dissolution of Mn creates a Mn/MnF2 redox buffer in the salt that fixes the potential at a level where Cr dissolution is thermodynamically unfavorable, while the loss of Mn from the alloy matrix drives the precipitation of a Cr-rich BCC phase.. Limitations: The study does not determine how much Mn in the salt is required to reach a satisfactory buffer level; it is not sufficient to draw conclusions about the role of high entropy of mixing and sluggish diffusion in corrosion behavior based on this single alloy; phase separation was not observed in previous studies because they were performed at lower temperatures or shorter times.. Future work: Further experimental results with various HEAs in different salt media are needed to better understand HEA behavior; the amount of Mn required to reach a satisfactory buffer level should be studied; long-term aging experiments are needed to assess HEA phase stability.. Quote: "Results show that the HEA lost a higher mass compared to the reference 316 H stainless steel due to the dissolution of Mn into the molten salt."

card: Paper card. Question: How do native oxidation, lattice distortion, and the resulting core–shell microstructure influence the ferromagnetism, saturation magnetization, coercivity, and electrical resistivity of CoCrFeNi-based high-entropy alloy thin films?. System: CoCrFeNi thin films (CoCrFeNithin, CoCrFeNithick), AlxCoCrFeNi (x = 0.1–0.5), and CoCrFeNiOx (x = 0.4, 0.8) high-entropy alloy thin films. Processing: Radio frequency (RF) magnetron sputtering on single-crystal Si (100) substrates; background vacuum < 3.0 × 10−4 Pa; substrate temperature ≤ 323 K; Ar pressure ≈ 1.4 Pa (30 sccm); RF power 100–110 W; native oxidation occurred during/after deposition; O-incorporated films prepared with O2/Ar mixture at 0.3 Pa working pressure. Test conditions: Room temperature (298 K); in-plane magnetic hysteresis loops measured by vibrating sample magnetometer; electrical resistivity measured by four-point probe; microstructure and composition analyzed by SEM, TEM, XRD, EPMA, EDS-TEM, APT, and XPS; magnetic domains imaged by magnetic force microscopy. Findings: CoCrFeNithick film achieved a saturation magnetization (MS) of 667 emu cm−3 and a coercivity (HC) of 0.12 kA m−1, while CoCrFeNithin film showed MS = 445 emu cm−3 and HC = 1.55 kA m−1.; O-incorporated CoCrFeNiO0.4 film exhibited an electrical resistivity of 237 µΩ·cm, MS of 535 emu cm−3, and HC of 23 A m−1.; The CoCrFeNithick film displayed the highest initial permeability (µi = 466), whereas AlxCoCrFeNi films showed µi decreasing to 27 with increasing Al concentration.; Native oxidation created a core–shell structure where ferromagnetic Fe, Co, and Ni form the core and Cr oxide acts as a shell layer around columnar crystals.; The electrical resistivity of CoCrFeNithin (335.0 ± 2.09 µΩ·cm) was significantly higher than that of CoCrFeNithick (153.0 ± 4.52 µΩ·cm) due to increased grain boundaries and microcracks.; The FCC phase in the films exhibited ferromagnetism at room temperature due to severe lattice distortion, contrary to the paramagnetic behavior of bulk FCC CoCrFeNi alloys.; Magnetic domain sizes in CoCrFeNithick film were ≈65 nm, smaller than the ≈90 nm domains observed in other films.. Mechanism: Ferromagnetism arises from severe lattice distortion in the non-equilibrium thin films, which alters the exchange interaction distance (d–δ) to weaken antiferromagnetic Cr–Cr interactions and strengthen ferromagnetic Fe–Fe, Co–Co, and Ni–Ni interactions in the FCC phase. The native oxidation of Cr creates a core–shell structure that further enhances ferromagnetism by reducing Cr–Cr pairs, introducing ferromagnetic Cr–O–Cr interactions, and increasing the concentration of ferromagnetic elements in the core. Coercivity is dominated by complex magnetic anisotropy (macroscopic shape, columnar crystal, magneto-crystalline, and stress anisotropy) and is inversely related to magnetic domain size and the ratio of anisotropy energy to saturation magnetization (EA/MS).. Limitations: The text notes that theoretical results for bulk HEAs cannot be directly applied to HEATFs due to differences in coordination numbers, lattice constants, and valence electron distributions. Additionally, residual stress generated during fabrication significantly affects magnetic properties, and the presence of microcracks in thinner films increases coercivity.. Future work: The authors propose that the films can be employed to develop soft magnetic electronic devices due to their large composition- and performance-modulation ranges, and suggest that the native oxidation mechanism could be further explored to optimize composite effects.. Quote: "The core–shell structure enables a high saturation magnetization, enhances the electrical resistivity, and thus reduces the eddy‐current loss."

Paper card. Question: How do native oxidation and the addition of Al or O affect the soft magnetic properties and electrical resistivity of CoCrFeNi-based high-entropy alloy thin films?. System: CoCrFeNi-based HEATFs, specifically CoCrFeNi and CoCrFeNiO0.4, with variations involving Al and O additions. Processing: Preparation of soft magnetic CoCrFeNi thin films with FCC and BCC dual-phases via a method resulting in native oxidation. Findings: CoCrFeNiO0.4 film exhibited an electrical resistivity of 237 µΩ·cm; CoCrFeNiO0.4 film showed a saturation magnetization of 535 emu cm−3; CoCrFeNiO0.4 film demonstrated a coercivity of 23 A m−1; Addition of O increases both electrical resistivity (ρ) and saturation magnetization/coercivity (MS/HC); Addition of Al appropriately increases ρ but slightly reduces MS/HC; The films possess a native oxidation-produced core–shell structure with a ferromagnetic core (Fe, Co, Ni) and a Cr oxide shell. Mechanism: The ferromagnetism is determined by reinforced exchange interaction due to lattice distortion, weakened antiferromagnetic exchange due to preferential Cr oxidation, and contribution from the BCC phase; coercivity is associated with complex magnetic anisotropy and domain wall sizes; preferential Cr oxidation promotes the core–shell structure, adjusting the ratio between ferromagnetic and high-resistivity phases. Limitations: A detailed study on the evaluation of the effect of O addition on the soft magnetic properties is ongoing, and the corresponding results will be reported in the future. Future work: A detailed study on the evaluation of the effect of O addition on the soft magnetic properties is ongoing, and the corresponding results will be reported in the future. Quote: "The CoCrFeNiO0.4 film showed the best properties, with an electrical resistivity of 237 µΩ·cm, a saturation magnetization of 535 emu cm−3 and a coercivity of 23 A m−1."

card: Paper card. Question: How can High-Entropy Alloys (HEAs) be designed and optimized to simultaneously achieve high saturation magnetization, high electrical resistivity, and high malleability for soft magnetic material applications?. System: FeCoNi(AlSi)x where x ranges from 0 to 0.8 in molar ratio (alloys denoted A0 to A8). Processing: Arc-melting pure elements (>99.5 wt.% purity) in high-purity argon atmosphere on a water-cooled Cu hearth, remelted four times for homogeneity; rapid solidification into ingots; compressive testing of cylindrical samples (Φ3 × 6 mm) at room temperature with a strain rate of 2 × 10−4 s−1. Test conditions: Room temperature compressive testing; X-ray diffraction (30 kV, 20 mA, Cu target, 10°/min); Electrical resistivity measurement; Magnetization curves via Physical Property Measurement System (PPMS); SEM-EDS microstructural analysis. Findings: The optimal balance of properties is achieved at x = 0.2 (A2 alloy) with saturation magnetization of 1.15 T, coercivity of 1,400 A/m, electrical resistivity of 69.5 μΩ·cm, yield strength of 342 MPa, and strain without fracture of 50%.; Saturation magnetization (Ms) drops almost monotonically from 1.315 T at x = 0 (A0) to 0.46 T at x = 0.8 (A8) upon Al and Si addition.; Alloys with x ≤ 0.2 exhibit a single-phase FCC solid solution, while x = 0.3 shows a BCC + FCC mixture, and x ≥ 0.4 transitions to almost entirely BCC structure.; Plastic deformation (εp) exceeds 50% without fracture for x in the range of 0 to 0.2, whereas ductility diminishes significantly for x ≥ 0.4, with A8 shattering immediately after elastic deformation.; Electrical resistivity generally increases from x = 0 to x = 0.8, reaching 69.5 μΩ·cm at x = 0.2, which falls within the typical range (50–80 μΩ·cm) of silicon steels.; The A3 alloy (x = 0.3) exhibits a yield strength of 938 MPa and ultimate tensile strength of 2,857 MPa with 33% plasticity, attributed to the mixture of FCC and BCC phases.; Coercivity (Hc) is low for x ≤ 0.2 but increases dramatically at x = 0.3 due to phase boundaries hindering domain-wall movement, before falling back at x = 0.5.. Mechanism: High saturation magnetization in FCC structures is attributed to higher atomic packing density (more ferromagnetic atoms per unit volume) and the absence of anti-parallel magnetic coupling elements like Cr; electrical resistivity increases due to lattice distortion from Al/Si, chemical randomness acting as point defects, and electron scattering; mechanical strength and malleability are governed by the phase composition (FCC favors plasticity, BCC increases lattice resistance) and solid-solution strengthening from lattice distortion.. Limitations: The text notes that for x ≥ 0.4, ductility diminishes and samples become brittle; the A8 alloy shatters immediately after elastic deformation; coercivity is highly sensitive to microstructure and difficult to predict solely from composition; ab initio calculations systematically overestimate saturation magnetization compared to experiments due to limited system size and ignored impurities/phase segregation.. Future work: The authors suggest that coercivity can be tuned within a wide range at a given composition by controlling quenching rates and applying heat/pressure treatments to further reduce Hc; the insights on composition-dependent structures and properties can guide the design of structural and functional HEAs and the development of high-entropy soft magnetic materials.. Quote: "the optimal balance of magnetic, electrical, and mechanical properties is achieved at x = 0.2, for which the combination of saturation magnetization (1.15 T), coercivity (1,400 A/m), electrical resistivity (69.5 μΩ·cm), yield strength (342 MPa), and strain without fracture (50%) makes the alloy an excellent SMM."

card: Paper card. Question: How does the Al concentration (3.5 to 54 at.%) influence phase formation and magnetic properties in FeMnCoCrAl high entropy alloy thin films?. System: FeMnCoCrAl high entropy alloy thin films with Al content varying from 3.5 to 54 at.%. Processing: Co-sputtering of equiatomic FeMn, Co, Cr, and Al targets on Si (100) and Al2O3 (0001) substrates; power density varied from 2 to 7.5 W cm−2 for Al target; base pressure 2 × 10−5 Pa; Ar gas at 0.4 Pa; deposition time 22 min; substrate temperature <80 °C. Test conditions: Room temperature magnetic hysteresis (VSM, 5 T max field), temperature-dependent magnetization (10 mT field), XRD (grazing incidence, Co Kα), EDX, Atom Probe Tomography (60 K, 30 pJ laser pulse), TEM (200 kV), electrical resistivity (four-point probe, Van-der-Pauw method). Findings: Al additions to FeMnCoCr (α-Mn structure) induce formation of a body-centered cubic (BCC) phase, with a single BCC random solid solution forming at 8 at.% Al.; The largest saturation magnetization (Ms) of 82 Am2/kg was measured for the film containing 8 at.% Al.; Increasing Al concentration beyond 8 at.% causes a continuous decrease in Ms, dropping to 37 Am2/kg at 20 at.% Al and 7 Am2/kg at 40 at.% Al.; Thin films with Al concentrations of 26 at.% and 40 at.% exhibit nanoscale chemical separation (Al-Co rich regions) not resolved by standard XRD.; The 8 at.% Al single BCC phase thin film possesses a Curie temperature (Tc) greater than 900 K.; The coercivity (Hc) decreases from 13 mT at 4 at.% Al to 2.1 mT at 40 at.% Al, correlating with a reduction in column width from ~54 nm to ~20 nm.; The single phase BCC film containing 8 at.% Al exhibits an electrical resistivity of 151 µΩ cm, which increases with higher Al concentrations.. Mechanism: Al additions stabilize the BCC phase over the FCC phase by forming a pseudogap at the Fermi level. The increase in Ms at low Al content is due to the formation of the ferromagnetic BCC phase, while the subsequent decrease is caused by the dilution of ferromagnetic species (Fe, Co) by paramagnetic Al and lattice distortions from Al's larger atomic radius. Nanoscale segregation in high-Al films further reduces magnetization by reducing ferromagnetic exchange interactions.. Limitations: The thin film synthesis involves high quenching rates, so the composition boundaries for phase formation might deviate from those obtained by near-equilibrium processing. The study notes that more detailed investigations on factors affecting coercivity and magnetic anisotropy are subject of future work.. Future work: More detailed investigations on factors affecting Hc and the effects of magnetic anisotropy are subject of future work. The authors also suggest the material system may enable applications in magneto-caloric devices or high-frequency inductors.. Quote: "Al additions to FeMnCoCr crystallizing in the alpha-Mn structure cause the formation of the body centered cubic (BCC) structure."

card: Paper card. Question: How can a unique five-element Co–Cu–Fe–Ni–Zn high entropy alloy thin film be synthesized in a single step to achieve soft magnetic properties with high saturation magnetization and low coercivity, overcoming the challenges of anomalous deposition and phase control in aqueous media?. System: Co–Cu–Fe–Ni–Zn high entropy alloy (near equi-atomic composition). Processing: Pulse electrodeposition in aqueous medium at ~45 ºC; optimized parameters: forward ON time 50 ms, OFF time 10 ms, applied potential 1.5 V (potentiostatic mode), using sodium citrate as complexing agent and boric acid as buffer.. Test conditions: Room temperature characterization; Magnetic properties measured via Vibrating Sample Magnetometry (VSM) and Ferromagnetic Resonance (FMR) from 9 to 18 GHz; Microstructure analyzed via FESEM, STEM-EDS, 2D X-ray diffraction, and HRTEM.. Findings: The fabricated Co–Cu–Fe–Ni–Zn HEA thin films exhibited a saturation magnetization (Ms) of ~82 emu/g.; The films showed a relatively low coercivity (Hc) of 19.5 Oe and a remanent magnetization (Mr) of 1.17%.; The alloy hosts nanocrystalline features with a grain size ranging from ~5 to 20 nm.; The films possess a dual-phase structure consisting of Face Centered Cubic (FCC) and Body Centered Cubic (BCC) phases.; FMR measurements yielded a 4πMs value of ~16,136 Oe, indicating potential for microwave device applications.; The composition was found to be uniform throughout the film with no different chemical compositions in FCC and BCC grains.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the soft magnetic behavior and high saturation magnetization to the crystalline nature of the films (FCC/BCC dual phases) and the high concentration of ferromagnetic elements (Fe, Co, Ni) relative to diamagnetic elements (Cu, Zn). The pulse electrodeposition technique controls the reduction of five metal ions uniformly by managing the local pH, minimizing hydroxide formation, and reducing residual stresses, which facilitates the formation of nanocrystalline grains and twins with low stacking fault energy.. Limitations: The text notes that the composition of the HEA thin films varies slightly between STEM-EDS (single location) and FESEM-EDS (multiple locations) due to local heterogeneities and length scale differences, though the overall distribution is confirmed to be within the HEA range.. Future work: The authors propose that additional tuning of the electrodeposition parameters and the relative composition of the constituent elements can further reduce the coercivity of the thin film.. Quote: "The fabricated Co–Cu–Fe–Ni–Zn HEA thin films exhibited high saturation magnetization value of ~ 82 emu/g, relatively low coercivity value of 19.5 Oe and remanent magnetization of 1.17%."

card: Paper card. Question: Can high-entropy oxides with a disordered B-site configuration be successfully synthesized in the Ruddlesden–Popper structure, and how does the high-entropy arrangement affect the influence of the A-site lanthanide cation on material properties?. System: LnSr(Co,Fe,Ga,Mn,Ni)O4+δ where Ln = La, Pr, Nd, Sm, or Gd. Processing: Modified Pechini sol-gel method using nitrate salts, citric acid, and ethylene glycol; calcination at 700 °C for 6 h; uniaxial pressing of 10 mm pellets; sintering at 1200 °C for 20 h followed by slow cooling at 2 °C/min. Test conditions: XRD at room temperature and in situ high-temperature XRD up to 1000 °C; SEM/EDX at 15 kV; oxygen non-stoichiometry via iodometric titration and thermogravimetric analysis (RT–800 °C in synthetic air); total conductivity via 4-probe DC method (25–900 °C); Seebeck coefficient measurement; thermal expansion via dilatometry (25–900 °C). Findings: Three compositions (Pr, Nd, Sm) are phase-pure with I4/mmm symmetry, while La and Gd contain minor secondary phases (5.2 wt% and 0.4 wt%, respectively).; Oxygen non-stoichiometry (δ) is nearly identical across the series, ranging from 0.006 to 0.015, showing no correlation with A-site cation size.; Total conductivity ranges from 2.45 to 4.28 S/cm, with the Sm-based composition exhibiting the highest value.; Thermal expansion coefficients are remarkably similar across the series, varying between 14.55 and 15.21 × 10−6 K−1.; All materials display semiconducting behavior with negative Seebeck coefficients ranging from −50 to −130 μV/K.; SmSr(Co,Fe,Ga,Mn,Ni)O4+δ and NdSr(Co,Fe,Ga,Mn,Ni)O4+δ show full thermal stability up to 1000 °C with no secondary phase formation.; The sequence of conductivity (Sm > Nd > La > Pr > Gd) correlates directly with the sequence of room-temperature Seebeck coefficients.. Mechanism: The high-entropy arrangement of B-site cations imposes a dominant influence on the material properties, suppressing the typical strong dependence on the A-site lanthanide ion. The negative Seebeck coefficient is explained by the Fermi level being situated within the bandgap where hole effective masses are higher than electron effective masses, despite p-type conductivity. The low oxygen non-stoichiometry suggests the B-site configuration stabilizes the oxygen content more than the A-site selection.. Limitations: The study notes that it is impossible to determine at this stage whether the observed unique behaviors are applicable to all high-entropy RP oxides or are specific to the studied series. Additionally, the La-based material had high secondary phase content affecting density measurements, and the Ga content in EDX analysis showed higher error due to spectral overlap.. Future work: The authors propose that more extensive studies into the temperature dependence of magnetic properties should follow to fully explain the observed phenomena regarding conductivity and Seebeck coefficients.. Quote: "The results indicate a smaller impact of the lanthanide cation type on the properties than has typically been reported for conventional Ruddlesden–Popper type oxides, which may result from the high-entropy arrangement of the B-site cations."

card: Paper card. Question: Can epitaxial strain selectively stabilize specific magneto-electronic states and control spin orientation in chemically complex high entropy oxides (HEOs) despite local chemical heterogeneity?. System: (Co0.2Cr0.2Fe0.2Mn0.2Ni0.2)3O4 spinel high entropy oxide (HEO) thin films. Processing: Laser pulsed deposition (PLD) at 690 °C in 0.03 mbar oxygen pressure using a KrF excimer laser (248 nm, 5 Hz, 1.55 J cm−2) on MgO (001), STO (001), and MAO (001) substrates to induce tensile, relaxed, and compressive strain states respectively; films cooled at 20 °C min−1. Test conditions: Magnetic measurements at 5 K and 300 K using SQUID magnetometry; Magnetic Force Microscopy (MFM) at room temperature; Structural characterization via XRD, XRR, RSM, AFM, and TEM. Findings: The film on MgO exhibits tensile strain (ε = +0.97%) resulting in an in-plane easy axis and a hard out-of-plane (OOP) axis with linear M-H curves up to 70 kOe.; The film on MAO exhibits compressive strain (ε = −3.19%) resulting in perpendicular magnetic anisotropy (PMA) with an OOP easy axis and a square-like hysteresis loop.; The film on STO is relaxed (ε ≈ −0.4%) and displays isotropic magnetization behavior similar to bulk HEO.; A unique coexistence of fully coherent spinel and rocksalt HEO phases is observed in all films with no detectable chemical segregation.; MFM reveals a maze-like domain structure in compressively strained films, indicative of OOP magnetic anisotropy.; Tensile strain increases the hardness of the OOP axis significantly, while compressive strain creates an easy OOP magnetization.; The magnetic transition temperature remains well above room temperature across all strain states.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the strain-driven spin reorientation to magneto-elastic coupling where spin-orbit interaction (L orb × S) couples the partially quenched orbital moments of Co and Ni ions to the crystal field; compressive strain aligns the easy axis OOP, while tensile strain aligns it in-plane.. Limitations: The exact ratio of rocksalt-HEO to spinel-HEO phases is difficult to quantify; the specific reason for the universal formation of dual phases in thin films versus bulk remains an open question; the precise ion distribution and charge states in the epitaxial films cannot be readily obtained due to chemical complexity.. Future work: Further investigation is needed to understand the origin and mechanism related to the rocksalt-HEO phase formation in (Co0.2Cr0.2Fe0.2Mn0.2Ni0.2)3O4 epitaxial thin films and the thermodynamics of HEOs.. Quote: "Epitaxial strain can selectively stabilize specific magnetoelectronic states, despite the extreme local chemical and bonding heterogeneity of HEOs."

Question: How can the design principles of metastable β-Ti alloys be converged with high-entropy/medium-entropy alloys to achieve both high yield strength and low elastic modulus for biomedical implants?. System: Ti-Zr-Nb-Ta-Mo, Ti-Zr-Nb-Ta, Ti-Zr-Hf-Nb-Ta, Ti-V-Mo, Ti-V-Zr-Mo, and Ti-rich variants (e.g., Ti65-Zr20-Nb10-Mo5, Ti35-Zr27.5-Hf27.5-Nb5-Ta5). Processing: Casting (as-cast), annealing (e.g., 1000 °C for 168 h), and thermodynamic simulation using FactSage, Pandat, and Thermo-Calc to adjust compositions for phase stability and segregation reduction. Test conditions: Potentiodynamic polarization in simulated body fluid, compression and tensile testing, cell culture tests (osteoblasts), X-ray diffraction (XRD), SAED-TEM, and EPMA-WDS mapping. Findings: Equiatomic Ti-Zr-Nb-Ta-Mo HEA exhibited a compressive yield strength of 1330 MPa but suffered from severe dendritic segregation and a high elastic modulus.; Ti-Zr-Nb-Ta MEA (quaternary) achieved a compressive strain of 48 ± 6% and yield strength >1000 MPa, surpassing Ti-6Al-4V (970 MPa).; Ti65-Zr20-Nb10-Mo5 alloy showed the lowest elastic modulus (86 GPa) among Ti-rich MEAs and a yield strength of 1381 MPa.; Metastable Ti65-Zr18-Nb16-Mo1 ([Mo]eq ≈ 10) achieved high yield strength (>1100 MPa) and a lower elastic modulus (~60 GPa).; Ti45-Zr45-Nb5-Ta5 MEA (VEC = 4.18) exhibited a low elastic modulus of 57 GPa.; Increasing Ti content in Tix-Nb-Mo-Ta-W HEAs increased yield strength by 31% (Ti1 vs Ti0.25) and improved compressive deformability.; Ti1.4-Zr1.4-Nb0.6-Ta0.6-Mo0.6 HEA showed osteoblasts with more pseudopodia and longer focal adhesions compared to commercially pure Ti.. Mechanism: The authors argue that reducing the valence electron concentration (VEC) to 4.0–4.2 or the Mo equivalent ([Mo]eq) to below 10 wt% induces a metastable β-phase, which lowers the elastic modulus. Simultaneously, the high-entropy effects (lattice distortion, solid solution strengthening) and Ti-rich compositions enhance yield strength. Reducing the atomic size misfit (δ) and mixing enthalpy (ΔHmix) near zero minimizes compositional segregation and prevents intermetallic formation, thereby improving ductility and corrosion resistance.. Limitations: Severe compositional segregation persists in many equiatomic and non-equiatomic HEAs/MEAs, leading to high elastic modulus, reduced ductility, and decreased corrosion resistance. The Ms theory may not be applicable to HEAs/MEAs, and some alloys with high Ti content still exhibit segregation. The presence of Laves phases or secondary BCC phases can adversely affect mechanical properties.. Future work: Developing metastable β HEAs/MEAs that combine high strength and low modulus; surface modification of Ti-containing HEAs to induce bioactivity (e.g., anodization, hydroxyapatite deposition); further investigation into the relationship between thermodynamic parameters and modulus; and reducing segregation through optimized composition design.. Quote: "To satisfy the demands of biomedical implants, researchers have sought to synthesize the strengths of high-entropy alloys and metastable β-Ti alloys, culminating in the development of metastable high-entropy/medium-entropy alloys that manifest both high strength and a low elastic modulus."

card: Paper card. Question: How to rapidly design low-cost Co-free Al-Cr-Fe-Ni FCC/B2-structured eutectic medium entropy alloys (EMEAs) with excellent mechanical and corrosion properties?. System: Al-Cr-Fe-Ni system, specifically AlCr1.18FeNi2.8 and AlCrFe1.46Ni2.5 alloys. Processing: Vacuum arc melting under pure argon atmosphere; raw materials >99.9 wt% purity; remelted at least five times; solidified in a water-cooled copper hearth (18 mm diameter, 12 mm thickness). Test conditions: Compressive tests at 1 × 10−3 s−1 strain rate; electrochemical tests in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution at 25 °C; potentiodynamic polarization scan rate 1 mV/min; EIS from 105 to 10−2 Hz. Findings: Mathematical rules established: c ≥ 1.0, 4.38a + 4.28b + 3.97c ≈ 20.55, and c − a ˃ 1.0.; Both alloys exhibit lamellar eutectic microstructure with FCC and ordered B2 (B2) phases.; Volume ratio of B2 to FCC phase (VB2/VFCC) is 0.605 for AlCr1.18FeNi2.8 and 0.679 for AlCrFe1.46Ni2.5.; Yield stress higher than 500 MPa and compressive fracture strength higher than 2450 MPa.; Fracture strain > 40% for both alloys.; AlCr1.18FeNi2.8 shows better corrosion resistance with Ecorr of −436 mV and Icorr of 7.42 μA∙cm−2.; Cr-rich spherical nanoparticles segregate within the B2 phase matrix.; L12 nanoprecipitates are found within the FCC phase of AlCrFe1.46Ni2.5.. Mechanism: The unique lamellar microstructure allows coordinated deformation: soft FCC phase undergoes initial plastic deformation while hard B2 phase remains elastic, piling up dislocations at interfaces; Cr-rich BCC nanoprecipitates further hinder dislocation movement, improving strength and strain-hardening. Better corrosion resistance in AlCr1.18FeNi2.8 is attributed to the higher volume fraction of the FCC phase and higher nickel content.. Limitations: The text notes that traditional trial-and-error methods are time-consuming and have low success rates, though the proposed rule addresses this; no specific limitations of the current study's results are explicitly stated by the authors beyond the general challenge of industrial application for Co-containing alloys which this work aims to solve.. Future work: The authors state that the established rule has great potential in the composition design of EHEAs and imply further application of this rule to design more alloys, but do not explicitly list specific future experiments in the 'future work' section.. Quote: "The mathematical formulas are c ≥ 1.0, 4.38a + 4.28b + 3.97c ≈ 20.55, and c − a ˃ 1.0."
W4312187064.title: Rapid Design, Microstructures, and Properties of Low-Cost Co-Free Al-Cr-Fe-Ni Eutectic Medium Entropy Alloys

card: Paper card. Question: How does substituting Cr with V to tune atomic volume misfit affect the magnetic order and electric transport properties (specifically strange metallicity) in the CoNi(Cr/V) medium-entropy alloy system?. System: Ternary equiatomic CoNiCr (CNC), CoNi(Cr0.5V0.5) (CNCV), and CoNiV (CNV) medium-entropy alloys. Processing: Arc melting of high-purity elements, homogenization at 1100 °C for 24 hrs in Ar followed by water quenching, cold rolling to ~75% thickness reduction, and solutionizing at 1000 °C for 60 min followed by water quenching. Test conditions: Magnetization and electrical transport measurements performed in the temperature range of 5–335 K using a vibrating sample magnetometer (VSM) and 4-probe method. Findings: All three compositions exhibited a single-phase face-centered cubic (FCC) crystal structure with lattice parameters of 3.576 ± 0.004 Å (CNC), 3.598 ± 0.002 Å (CNCV), and 3.617 ± 0.002 Å (CNV).; Magnetic moments at 5 K were extremely small: 0.005 μB/f.u. for CNC, 0.007 μB/f.u. for CNCV, and 0.002 μB/f.u. for CNV.; The CoNiCr system displayed linear temperature dependence of resistivity (ρ(T) = ρ0 + ρ1 T), indicative of strange metallicity.; Vanadium-substituted samples (CNCV and CNV) required an additional electron-electron scattering term (ρ2 T2) to fit resistivity data, suggesting a deviation from pure quantum criticality.; Coercive fields for all alloys ranged from 30 to 60 Gauss (2.4–4.8 kA/m), classifying them as semihard magnets.; Residual resistivity ratio (RRR) monotonically decreased with increasing Vanadium substitution, indicating higher residual resistivity.; No significant magnetoresistance was observed in any of the samples.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the small magnetic moments and strange metallicity to magnetically driven chemical short-range order (SRO) and magnetic frustration. They propose that complex interactions between ferromagnetic Co/Ni and antiferromagnetic Cr/V create unbalanced magnetic sublattices (ferrimagnetism), where the frustration of magnetic moments leads to the observed linear resistivity and quantum critical behavior.. Limitations: The ferrimagnetic Curie temperature was not determined due to setup limitations preventing high-temperature measurements, and the authors note that direct experimental evidence of SRO remains intangible without advanced tools like muon spin resonance.. Future work: The authors suggest that careful experimental tools such as muon spin resonance and/or neutron reflectivity are needed to shed light on the magnetic short-range order driven by a state of frustration.. Quote: "The electric transport measurements revealed a strange metallicity evidenced through the observation of the linear temperature dependence of the resistivity."
