card: Paper card. Question: How does the biocompatibility of a Ti-rich medium-entropy alloy (Ti65M) compare to a Ti-alloy (TNSM) and commercially pure titanium (CP-Ti) regarding glioblastoma astrocytoma cell viability, morphology, and gene expression?. System: Ti65-Zr18-Nb16-Mo1 (Ti65M), Ti-13Nb-7Sn-4Mo (TNSM), and commercially pure titanium (CP-Ti). Processing: Arc-melting and casting system (A-028, Dawn Shine, New Taipei City, Taiwan); samples cut into discs (10 mm diameter, 1 mm height); surfaces abraded to #1500 silicon carbide papers; cleaned ultrasonically with alcohol, acetone, and deionized water. Test conditions: U-87 MG glioblastoma astrocytoma cells (1 × 10^4 cells) seeded on 1.2 cm diameter samples; incubated for 24 h, then replated for an additional 24 h prior to MTT tests; extracts tested via PBS wash; contact angles measured with 1μL deionized water; XRD (40 kV, 40 mA, 2θ = 20–90°); AFM (5 × 5 μm2 scanning range). Findings: Ti65M exhibited the highest hardness (366.5 ± 3.6 HV) and lowest average roughness (38 ± 8 nm), while CP-Ti had the lowest hardness (172.3 ± 4.4 HV) and highest roughness (94 ± 26 nm).; All three materials were hydrophilic, with CP-Ti having the lowest contact angle (46.0 ± 0.9°) compared to Ti65M (54.3 ± 2.0°).; Cell viability on Ti65M and TNSM (β structures) was considerably higher than on CP-Ti (α' structure), with viability decreasing as Ti content increased.; U-87 MG cells showed the highest number of dendrites and axons on Ti65M, with significantly fewer observed on TNSM and CP-Ti.; Expression of ERK was reduced on TNSM and CP-Ti substrates compared to Ti65M, potentially causing lower cell migration and proliferation.; Higher expression of p53 and NFkβ was observed in U-87 MG cells on CP-Ti compared to other alloys, suggesting CP-Ti may induce apoptosis.; All extract viabilities exceeded 90%, indicating low indirect cytotoxicity for all three materials.. Mechanism: The authors propose that the superior biocompatibility of Ti65M is related to its high content of Zr and Nb elements, which are highly biocompatible and exhibit low cytotoxicity. Additionally, the metastable β-phase structure and high hardness improve wear resistance, preventing accelerated release of metal ions. The lower expression of p53 on Ti65M compared to CP-Ti suggests reduced apoptosis, while higher expression of growth factor pathway genes (RAS, ERK, S6) on Ti65M correlates with increased cell growth and migration.. Limitations: The authors state that the mechanisms connecting surface roughness and hydrophilicity to cellular adhesion, growth, autophagy, and differentiation are not yet clear. They also note that phase structure alone is insufficient to explain viability differences and that further investigation of corrosion resistance is needed.. Future work: The authors propose that increased cell migration on Ti65M is a subject for further study and that further investigation of the corrosion resistance of Ti65M and TNSM will be reported in future studies.. Quote: "Ti65M has an ultra-low elastic modulus (61 GPa) due to its metastable state, which is significantly lower than those of Ti-64 (110 GPa) [] and TZNTM HEA (153 GPa) []."

card: Paper card. Question: What is the magnetic state that develops in the highly structurally and chemically inhomogeneous Al28Co20Cr11Fe15Ni26 single-crystalline high-entropy alloy?. System: Al28Co20Cr11Fe15Ni26 single-crystalline high-entropy alloy (ACCFN). Processing: Czochralski monocrystal growth from a heterogeneous tungsten seed under 650 mbar Ar atmosphere at a pulling rate of 1 mm/h. Test conditions: Direct-current magnetization, hysteresis curves, alternating-current magnetic susceptibility, and thermoremanent magnetization time decay measured from 1.8 to 400 K; magnetic fields up to 7 T and 100 mT; AC frequencies 1–1000 Hz. Findings: The material consists of a B2 matrix (94 vol%) and spherical A2 nanoparticles (6 vol%) with an average diameter of 64 nm.; The Cr-free B2 matrix (Al28Co25Fe15Ni32) forms a disordered ferromagnetic state with a Curie temperature TC ≈ 390 K.; The A2 nanoparticles (Co19Cr56Fe25) exhibit a core-shell structure with CoFe-enriched shells of ~2 nm thickness.; The nanoparticle shells are ferromagnetic, while the nanoparticle cores are asperomagnetic (a subclass of spin glasses).; Asperomagnetism in the nanoparticle cores develops below a spin-freezing temperature Tf ≈ 15 K.; Below 15 K, the system exhibits broken-ergodicity phenomena, including a growing difference between zero-field-cooled and field-cooled magnetizations.; The low-temperature M(H) curve at 1.8 K shows a linear tail at high fields, confirming a minor antiferromagnetic component from the asperomagnetic cores.; No mictomagnetic (cluster glass) state was observed, as zfc and fc hysteresis curves perfectly overlapped at 6 K.. Mechanism: The B2 matrix contains only ferromagnetic elements (Co, Fe, Ni) leading to a disordered ferromagnetic state with positive exchange interactions. The A2 nanoparticles contain the antiferromagnetic element Cr alongside Co and Fe, creating mixed FM/AFM interactions. This results in a distribution of exchange interactions where FM interactions dominate but AFM interactions exist, forming an asperomagnetic state in the cores. The core-shell structure arises from CoFe enrichment at the A2–B2 interfaces. The asperomagnetic state is magnetically frustrated, leading to ergodicity breaking and spin freezing below 15 K.. Limitations: The ferromagnetic nature of the nanoparticle shells could not be verified experimentally by bulk magnetization measurements because their signal is masked by the much stronger ferromagnetic contribution from the B2 matrix.. Quote: "The results reveal that the Cr-free B2 matrix of composition Al28Co25Fe15Ni32 forms a disordered ferromagnetic (FM) state that undergoes an FM transition at TC≈ 390 K."

Question: How does the substitution of ferromagnetic Co with antiferromagnetic Cr, combined with annealing temperature, influence the hierarchical phase decomposition, microstructure, and resulting magnetic and mechanical properties in AlCoFeNi-based high entropy alloys?. System: AlCoFeNi (x=1) and AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi (x=0.5) high entropy alloys. Processing: Arc melting of elemental pellets (99.9% purity) under argon atmosphere followed by isothermal annealing at 600 °C and 1000 °C for 15 h and water quenching. Test conditions: Annealing at 600 °C/15 h and 1000 °C/15 h; characterization via SEM, EBSD, TEM, APT, Vickers microhardness, and magnetic saturation/coercivity measurements. Findings: AlCoFeNi annealed at 1000 °C forms a single ordered B2 phase with a microhardness of 406 VHN and saturation magnetization of 112 emu/g.; AlCoFeNi annealed at 600 °C decomposes into a B2 + BCC mixture with a microhardness of 474 VHN.; AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi annealed at 1000 °C exhibits coarse B2 + BCC phase separation with grain boundary FCC phases.; AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi annealed at 600 °C shows a hierarchical microstructure with decomposition length scales ranging from ~3–5 nm (APT) to ~50–100 nm (TEM) to micron-scale lamellae.; The AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi alloy annealed at 600 °C achieved the highest microhardness of 475 VHN.; Saturation magnetization of the Cr-containing alloy (AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi) is reduced by more than 50% compared to the Cr-free alloy due to the antiferromagnetic nature of Cr.; Coercivity decreases with increasing annealing temperature, dropping from 15 Oe at 600 °C to 4 Oe at 1000 °C for the AlCoFeNi alloy.; APT cluster analysis detected Cr-rich BCC precipitates with concentrations ranging from 16% to 74% depending on the generation scale.. Mechanism: The addition of Cr enhances phase separation due to the positive enthalpy of mixing in Fe-Cr, Co-Cr, and Ni-Cr systems, which creates miscibility gaps, whereas the Al-Cr system has a negative enthalpy of mixing favoring compound formation; the length scale of decomposition is controlled by the interplay of composition and annealing temperature.. Limitations: The thermodynamic model predicted an FCC phase in AlCoFeNi at 1000 °C which was not observed experimentally, likely due to a high nucleation barrier; the specific thermodynamic basis for Cr's influence on phase separation in these complex multi-component alloys requires further analysis beyond the scope of the paper.. Future work: Further detailed investigation is required to understand the relationship between B2 phase decomposition into a two-phase B2 + BCC microstructure and the resulting coercivity; the details of the thermodynamic basis underlying the influence of Cr on phase separation require analysis beyond the current scope.. Quote: "The length scale of this decomposition is determined by the combination of composition and annealing temperature."

card: Paper card. Question: How do longitudinal spin fluctuations (LSFs) influence the magnetic structure, phase stability, stacking fault energy, and interfacial energy of the paramagnetic CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy across different temperatures and volumes?. System: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi (Cantor alloy) in face-centered cubic (fcc) and hexagonal close-packed (hcp) structures. Processing: First-principles alloy theory using density-functional theory (DFT) with the exact muffin-tin orbitals (EMTO) method, generalized gradient approximation (PBE), and the disordered local moment (DLM) picture combined with the coherent-potential approximation (CPA); LSFs modeled via the 'fluctuating medium approximation' and 'one shot from static equilibrium approach' over a temperature range of 50–1200 K and varying Wigner-Seitz radii.. Test conditions: Temperature range 50–1200 K; Wigner-Seitz radii varying to simulate lattice expansion; comparison between fcc and hcp crystal structures; inclusion of experimentally determined thermal lattice expansion.. Findings: LSFs induce sizable magnetic moments for Co, Cr, and Ni in both fcc and hcp phases, whereas these elements show zero or negligible moments in conventional floating spin (FS) calculations.; The hcp phase is energetically preferable to the fcc phase at low temperatures and small volumes, leading to negative stacking fault energy at cryogenic conditions.; The stacking fault energy (γisf) increases monotonically with temperature, rising from −17 mJ m−2 at 50 K to 31 mJ m−2 at 1000 K in the LSF scheme.; The critical temperature for the fcc-hcp phase transition at ambient pressure is predicted to be ~430 K in LSF calculations and ~438 K in FS calculations.; LSFs reduce the magnetic entropy contribution to the stacking fault energy but increase the internal energy contribution, with the positive temperature dependence of γisf dominated by magneto-volume coupling.; The fcc-hcp interfacial energy (σ) slightly decreases with temperature, varying in the range of ~3.1–6.0 mJ m−2 for LSF calculations between 50 and 1200 K.; The difference in mean magnetic moments between fcc and hcp phases is small, amounting to ~0.05–0.23 μB at 100 K and reducing further as temperature increases.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the temperature-dependent behavior to the interplay between magneto-volume coupling and longitudinal spin fluctuations. LSFs induce thermal magnetic moments in elements like Cr and Ni that are otherwise non-magnetic in static calculations, which alters the magnetic entropy and internal energy contributions to the free energy. The hcp phase becomes stable at low temperatures due to these energetic shifts, resulting in negative stacking fault energy that promotes nano-twin and stacking fault formation. As temperature rises, the stacking fault energy becomes positive, suppressing these defects.. Limitations: The explicit phonon effect is not considered in the theory, which may contribute to the discrepancy between the predicted critical temperature (~430 K) and the experimental value (~633 K). The structural relaxation in the faulted supercell was omitted, and an ideal c/a ratio of 8/3 was assumed for the hcp structure.. Future work: The text does not explicitly state future work proposed by the authors beyond the current study's scope.. Quote: "The hcp phase is energetically preferable to the fcc one at cryogenic temperatures, which results in negative stacking fault energy at these conditions."

card: Paper card. Question: What is the influence of a hierarchically decomposed B2 + A2 structure on the formation of magnetic vortex states and the origin of coercivity in AlCo(Cr)FeNi high-entropy alloys?. System: AlCoFeNi and AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi high-entropy alloys. Processing: Arc melting of Al, Co, Cr, Fe, and Ni pellets in an Ar atmosphere, followed by annealing at 600°C for 15 h in an Ar atmosphere and quenching in water. Test conditions: Bulk magnetization measured at 300 K up to 1 T; Lorentz TEM and off-axis electron holography performed in magnetic-field-free conditions and with applied out-of-plane fields up to 1.5 T; APT conducted at 60 K. Findings: AlCoFeNi has a saturation magnetization (MS) of 99.8 Am2/kg and coercivity (Hc) of 1.45 mT, while AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi has MS of 46.2 Am2/kg and Hc of 9.56 mT.; AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi exhibits a hierarchical structure with coarse A2 gen-1 (1–5 μm), medium A2 gen-2 (50-150 nm), and fine A2 gen-3 (<10 nm) phases in a B2 matrix.; A2 gen-2 precipitates in region R1 contain 3D magnetic vortex states with a magnetic induction peak of 0.5 ± 0.1 T.; The ratio of clockwise to counterclockwise magnetic vortices in A2 gen-2 precipitates is approximately 1:1 at remanence.; The A2 shell surrounding A2 gen-2 precipitates is 2 nm thick and has ~25% higher magnetization than the A2 gen-1 matrix in region R2.; Magnetic vortices in A2 gen-2 precipitates can reverse their rotation direction when exposed to external magnetic fields of 100–500 mT.; The B2 matrix in region R1 is weakly ferromagnetic and reverses its magnetization sign during magnetic switching.. Mechanism: The increased coercivity in AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi is attributed to a complex magnetization process involving the successive reversal of magnetic vortices within A2 precipitates and interactions with a weakly ferromagnetic B2 matrix, rather than simple domain wall pinning.. Limitations: The interactions between different magnetic elements remain unclear; off-axis electron holography cannot detect the magnetic vortex core direction; the study does not cover the effects of temperature, strain, or magnetic field on precipitate formation.. Future work: Future studies should determine the effect of external magnetic field and/or stress annealing, kinetics, and other external stimuli on precipitate formation to control magnetic anisotropy and properties; in situ magnetizing experiments and micromagnetic simulations are needed to address dynamic reversal processes.. Quote: "We reveal for the first time the influence of a hierarchically decomposed B2 + A2 structure in an AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi HEA on the formation of magnetic vortex states within individual A2 (disordered BCC) precipitates."
